**The meaning of the hadith**
In this great hadith — about which it has been said that it is a quarter of Islam, and one of four hadiths from which all good manners branch out — the Prophet ﷺ explains that complete faith is not achieved by any Muslim (the negation here is not meant to deny faith at its root, but to deny its completeness) until he loves for his brother the acts of obedience and the kinds of good in religion and worldly life that he loves for himself, and dislikes for him what he dislikes for himself. If he sees a shortcoming in his Muslim brother's religion, he strives to set it right; and if he sees good in him, he supports him and helps him to stay firm on it and do more of it. So the believer is not a true believer until he is pleased for people with what he is pleased with for himself. This only comes from a heart completely free of rancour, deceit and envy; for envy means that the envious person hates for anyone to surpass him in something good, or to equal him in it, because he loves to stand out above people with his virtues and to have them for himself alone. Faith requires the opposite: that all the believers share with him the good that Allah has given him.

📖 From the Hadith Encyclopedia — Dorar.net.

**Talk with your child**
1. Why was Rayyan sure that he would win? And what did he use to say to Anas as Anas repeated the ayah?
2. What did Rayyan do after the result was announced? And what question did his father ask that changed his heart?
3. Should Rayyan not have wished to win, or not have felt sad when he lost? (No, competing in good is praiseworthy, and feeling sad about losing is natural; what is blameworthy is hating for your brother to get something good, or wishing that it would be taken away from him.)

**This week's exercise**
Every day this week your child sincerely congratulates a brother, sister or friend on something they did well, and teaches someone something they themselves are good at, just as Rayyan and Anas began memorising together.
